title: Franma and the Mustard Seed
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching is about finding comfort and solace in Buddhism despite facing rejection and hardship throughout one's life. Nomon Tim Burnett shares personal stories of their family's history, including their grandmother Fran's journey from being scorned by her husband's family to finding peace through Buddhism, as well as a story about Kisa Gotani, an Indian woman who found refuge in Buddhism after being shunned by her community. Through these stories, Nomon highlights the importance of compassion and community in healing and coping with loss, emphasizing that even in difficult times, there is always the possibility for transformation and connection.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody.
Good to see you.
Usually every year in July I'm supposed to stop hovering around here, which is hard for me to do, but I do it and then I appreciate it once I get out the door.
This year during July I did several things.
I went on a solo backpack, just a couple of days with myself, and it was really wonderful.
I rediscovered something.
Some stress fell off.
It's amazing how we can carry stress.
We don't really notice it until it releases.
Then I went to our Zen monastery in this lineage, Tassajara Monastery in California, and I gave a workshop there on compassion for yourself.
That was nice.
Then I went to San Diego to see my family, which I'm going to speak about a little bit tonight, for a memorial weekend for my grandmother.
Then I came back for a second and turned around again and went to Portland, because I thought it would be a good place to experience the heat wave.
It worked out good, although John did better, I guess, by going to Utah.
Hotter there.
And there I was at a meeting of the American Zen Teachers Association.
Are you going to let me be okay with the fan on, or should we turn it off?
It's nice to have the air, huh?
Okay.
Who cares?
You can hear me.

I didn't really want to go, because I've been away so much, but I was really glad I went to that meeting, four days, with people from all over the country and different Zen lineages, not just our Soto Zen school but different stripes and varieties of Zen.
It was hosted at a Zen temple in a different lineage, a place called [unclear: "Dharma Reign Zen Community"], which is an amazing place.
I'll say more about that another time, but I really recommend it.
It's really great to be a Zen tourist and go to different centers.
It gives you a little more perspective on what we're doing here.
Colette and Jonathan were saying they were just Zen tourists too.
They went to the [unclear: "Greenville Farms Zen Center"] in California.
On the one hand, you appreciate the different ways that they do things in these different Zen places.
Like, kind of familiar, but kind of different.
Then your mind usually goes off on the stupid way that they do things, because it's not what you're used to, right?
So if it's not what you're used to, it must not be right.
Then your mind spins around from there and you say, what a dummy I am for thinking that.
It's perfectly legitimate.
I should respect diversity.
It's one of my favorite things about this whole enterprise that we take so seriously the particulars and details of the way we do things, because it matters and there's a feeling to it.
But it's great that we take it so seriously and that it doesn't matter at all.
It's completely arbitrary and made up, with some tradition to it.
But it's a tradition of making things up, is what it is.
You don't change it for a hundred years, then it becomes somehow a different kind of made up, but still made up.

I want to talk a little bit about my experience with the memorial ceremonies for my grandmother, and think a little bit about the fact that all families, without exception, no suffering, you know, no tragedy.
So here's a story from early Buddhism, at the time of the Buddha.
There is a young woman from a lower caste family.
It was a caste system in India then, and now.
Her name was Kisa Gotani.
Somehow she caught the eye of a man a little higher up in the hierarchy and they got married.
In those days, in that culture, the woman would go live with her husband's family.
So you're not just marrying him, you're entering into this whole other family with all his relatives and stuff.
They didn't like her very much.
They didn't think this was such a good thing.
Imagine how stressful that would be.
She was probably pretty young, living in this family and being scorned and ignored.
Maybe abused a little bit too.
It was especially bad because she was having trouble getting pregnant.
You're supposed to have a baby, right?
Finally she does.
She has a baby.
It wasn't recorded if it was a boy or a girl or a non-binary person.
We had friends we visited in California, and their younger child, who was their daughter, is now a non-binary person.
They are doing well, so that was interesting.
So finally they do have the child and things get a little better from there.
But then, of course, it's not uncommon if you have a child to lose a child.
The child dies somehow, and she completely loses her mind, in sorrow, in stress, in shame.
Really loses her mind.

She's actually wandering around the town carrying the body of the child, unable to put it down, unable to accept what has happened, muttering to herself and trying to get somebody to help her heal the child and bring the child back to life.
The story goes that an old man told her that she should see the Buddha.
The Buddha was around the town at the time, and the Buddha could help her.
The Buddha told her that yes, he could bring the child back if she could find a mustard seed from a family where no one had died.
She could bring back to him a mustard seed.
That would be the special medicine.
But a special kind of mustard seed, a mustard seed given to her by another family in which no one had died.
So she desperately went from house to house.
Of course, she couldn't find anybody like that.
Every family had known death, tragedy, and sorrow.
Finally, somehow, either before or after, in different versions of the story, she got back to the Buddha.
She realized, oh, this is just what is.
And she was freed in some way.
I'm sure she was still sad, but freed from the madness and the intense weight of her suffering, because she could accept that this is how it is.
This is how it is for humans and families, that there is always loss.
The story goes that she then also instantly had a great degree of lightening up.

In the way the old tradition is described, there are four big stages of awakening, and she just popped into the first stage of awakening and went on eventually to become a very steady and important nun and a student of the Buddha, and to awaken completely.
Sometime in the early 1940s, my grandmother, Fran, Frances Reeder, I can't remember how they met, but she met a man named Frank Burnett.
They got married.
Frank was an only child and very, very smart.
A little nervous disposition.
They probably said that in those days, a little nervous disposition.
They didn't really know about depression or anxiety, I guess, back then.
Does that mean it didn't exist if they didn't have those words?
Could be.
Could be the more we have these words, depression and anxiety, the more of it we have, I don't know.

Anyway, he was very smart and, like his son, my father, and myself in the end, got through school very quickly, did what he thought he was supposed to do, and sought approval through trying to be good and do it right.
He was a bookkeeper.
They moved together to Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, and he was a bookkeeper at the Bethlehem Steel Company, the biggest steel company in the world, producing steel for the building of America.
He had a terrible boss who put him down and scorned him and rejected him.
He was having more and more trouble surviving this job.
At one point, his boss moved his desk out into the hall, just to freak him out and shame him, so that he wasn't even allowed in the office.
Of course, he didn't say anything.
He just showed up and set down his lunchbox or something and did the accounts.
Then World War II happened and he entered the Army.
I don't know if he was drafted or volunteered.
He got a desk job, and the same damn stuff happened.
He was scorned and rejected and didn't fit in.
He was having a hard time.
Meanwhile, the family had three children, my father, my aunt, and my brother, and my uncle.
Then in the middle 50s, they decided to do what Americans always do when things aren't going right.
They went west to have a new start.
I guess we go to Hawaii.
They moved to San Diego.
I think he had a cousin there who helped him get a job, which was part of the reason why it wasn't completely without support.
But it really was a new place, new culture, new climate, from Pennsylvania, where they had both grown up.
I don't forget if my grandmother told me what happened in this new job, but some version of more of the same.
Being a vet, he went to the VA hospital and told them he was having a hard time.
I just learned this last week, two weeks ago, when I was down there: he was prescribed some kind of medication.
I can't remember the name of it.
Maybe Judith would know it if I can remember the name of it.
That apparently was itself a depressant.
It made him more depressed.
So I don't understand that, but they didn't understand very well how to treat depression.
Then one day in 1956, actually I know what day, August 12th, 1956, my uncle got up first and he was eating his breakfast cereal before going to school.
He was 11.
His sister, my aunt, was 13.
My father was 15.
Their dad was briefly in the kitchen.
Brian is my uncle.
Brian somehow felt like he should have engaged his dad in a conversation, but he didn't.
They sat together for a minute and his dad went to the garage, where he hanged himself.
A little while later, his mom, my grandmother, came down and said, "Where's your father?"
She couldn't find him, and eventually they did find him.
All the kids were there.
Their mom was screaming, "Bring me the sewing scissors.
Cut him down."
So this was a tragedy that marked all of their lives.
It somehow marked my life and my siblings' lives and probably my children's lives in some way.
When Fran died at the age of 98 in the spring, Brian, my uncle, had the idea somehow that this was sad, but this could also bring healing.
Somehow, mourning his mother's death.
They never called their mom "Mom" after that.
I don't know if it was right at that moment or a little later.
They always called her Fran.
So I never heard my uncle or aunt or my father ever say the word "mom."
Anyway, the idea was that Fran's death could somehow be a way of healing Frank's death.
Frank was buried in a military cemetery as a veteran, even though it was a suicide.
That was good, I think, of the military.
They kind of knew where it was, but I don't know if they'd never been there or they only went there once in a blue moon.
They told me that the kids didn't go to the funeral.
Just one day, father was not there.
My grandma Fran was somebody I was very close to.
She was very close to my mother, even though my mother and father eventually divorced.
They stayed very, very close, my mother's mother-in-law.
A lot of my upbringing was Fran coming over and talking to my mom in the kitchen and sharing these outrageous spiritual stories.
Somehow after she got through all this, later in the 50s and in the 60s, she got big into spirituality: yoga, faith healing, spirits, seances, Ouija boards, all of that.

I remember one time she went to Brazil to meet a faith healer and came back with these incredible stories, which I vaguely remember, of somebody with this terrible crippling disease and the Brazilian healer putting hands on the person, and a rainbow appeared and they could walk again.
I think it was what she experienced and what she saw.
She worked with an Indian teacher for a while.
I can't remember if she went to India or if she met him in New Jersey or something.
She talked about her Indian teacher.
One of the big Indian teachers, you would have heard of him, but I'm forgetting which one right now.
Once I started getting into Zen, she was very supportive.
She helped pay my fees to go to [unclear: "Gringold"] when I was 20 years old and had no money.
I especially wrote a lot of letters from the monastery, because it was before the internet, and there were no phones and we were completely cut off.
So we wrote lots of letters.
There were lots of letters to my wife and lots of letters to my girlfriend.
When we were getting ready for the memorial ceremony, my Uncle Brian emailed me to say, "You know what, I've been going through Fran's papers and she saved every letter you kids ever wrote her.
I've got this huge file of letters that you sent to her, Tim.
I'm going to send that to you."
A little while later this big, huge padded envelope showed up, and I didn't want to open it somehow.
I'm just not sure why.
When I opened it, it was fascinating, because it was 99.9% letters and cards, thank you cards and Christmas cards, mostly thank you cards.
Every one of them, from about the age of eight to the age of 25, started with basically the same sentence: "Dear Fran, I'm so sorry it's taken me so long to send you this thank you card."
There's one in maybe about a 12-year-old hand saying, "I guess I'm just a kind of person that it takes me a while to get to things.
But thank you very much.
I really liked the sweater," or the baseball, whatever it was.
It really bothered Fran that my birthday was close to Christmas.
I was born in early January.
So she would say we would celebrate my birthday on my half birthday in July.
So it's appropriate.
I suppose I was down there not that long after my half birthday in July, to think about that till now.

At one point, my cousin, who was very good at continuing to visit with her, much better than any of the rest of us, my young cousin, quite a bit younger than me, 15 years younger, said, "You know, Fran is really interested in what you're doing in Buddhism.
Please send her something."
Okay, okay.
So I took one of my Dharma talks and I wrote it up really nice and formatted it and put my picture on there.
I sent it to her.
I never heard anything back.
I'd forgotten I'd done it.
But in this stack of correspondence was this Dharma talk that I had sent her, and attached to the back of it was a poem that she wrote.
I must have sent this to her somewhere around 2003.
I was early on doing Dharma talks.
I've been doing Dharma talks, I guess, since soon after ordination in 2001.
It was an untitled poem and it was just dated.
It said, "August 12, 2003, on the 47th anniversary."
At first I didn't know what that meant. 47th anniversary of what?
You probably already figured that out.
So here's Fran's last poem.
It's 47 years today.
*47 years.
Oh, Frank, Frank, Frank. 47 years since you went, since you made the ugly choice.
Bid us goodbye as best you could.
With what little you had left and went. 47 years.
Why must I stay?
What service must I perform that I haven't yet sought out and done?*

*We were like two very intricate pieces of a jigsaw puzzle, you and I, who came together so long ago and found that with only slight adjustments, every furrow, every hillock, every aspect fitted to perfection.
We had the greatest miracle of life, we two.
We were completed by each other.
We were truly one. 47 years.
The aching loss I stored so deep in my psyche, a weight I carry with every step I make, every breath I take, will always be with me until we meet again.*
That was the writing by her that came back to me in 2017, 14 years after she wrote that, and somehow it was paper clipped to my talk, too.
No post-it, just there.
She was also very devoted to serving others.
She drove for Meals on Wheels.
She was a terrible driver, too.
That was one of the big topics at the memorial.
At one of the memorials, we talked about what an awful driver she was, and it was amazing if she had never killed anybody.
She would be very rageful and impatient, otherwise like a spiritual being.
You could put her behind a car and she'd just...
We went to visit her with Walker when he was about three, and she was still driving, so she was in her 80s, and she picked us up at the train station.
I regret to this day that we didn't take a cab.
It was really quite frightening, actually.
We were just like, it's not very far.
Probably if we say anything, it'll just make her more tense.
Traffic wasn't that bad, but she was like...
And she taught yoga, as I mentioned.
I thought she was completely self-taught, but I think she did have a very good yoga teacher.
They didn't really have yoga teacher training back then, so she took his class for a while and then set off teaching on her own.
She taught yoga from the age of about 40 to the age of 84, 44 years.
And at the end, she was teaching chair yoga at the over-60 trailer parks she lived in, with people who didn't have much mobility but really appreciated, I'm sure, her teaching.
So that's why it says in the poem, *"Why must I stay?
What service must I perform that I have not yet set out and done?"* She really did take care of people.
She drove people to appointments, and I'm sure did a little more healing on them than they necessarily requested.
I'm sure some of them did request it, but I'm convinced that many of them were like, I don't know if I want you to lay hands on me, lady.
But she could read your aura and tell you what was happening.
One time she told me, "Your aura is not really showing right now, Tim."
I wasn't worried about you.
Sorry.
I didn't know what to do.
So anyway, there were three memorial ceremonies, and I got all the information from my Uncle Brian that the family had invited me to officiate at all three.
The first was to be at the retirement home where she lived her last days, for the staff and her friends and other residents, a more public ceremony.
The next one, that very same night, two in one day, was to be at my uncle's house for family, more intimate.
And on the final morning of the weekend, there was to be a burial at sea.
There was a dinner before all this, too.
In the burial at sea and the other two memorial ceremonies, we had not just Fran's ashes.
My Uncle Brian had gone through a tremendous amount of paperwork to get his father exhumed from the cemetery.
We didn't know this, but according to the county death certificate, he had been cremated, so what was buried in a full-size plot in this military cemetery was just his ashes, he was told.
The cemetery had been full since 1966, when I was born, but there was a guy on duty sitting behind a desk from 1966 and for the rest of the time, I guess, just keeping an eye on things.
That's who you talk to, and he was really surprised and confused by this request, apparently, and put up a lot of resistance.
But finally Brian went over his head and did the stuff you've got to do.
I think there are a few ex-military people here.
Finally it came through, and they got a call and said, "The exhumation has been approved and we need you to now pay the fee."
And Uncle Brian's like, oh shit, the fee, what's this going to be?
And he said, "The fee is $36."
So we had on the little altar, very simple, just a table of flowers at the retirement home, and then I made a Zen altar at his house, and then at the boat.
At all of them, there were both of their ashes.
The first time we got there, it was an informal dinner of my cousins, and every one of the three siblings wanted to talk to me separately about what should or shouldn't happen.
Every one of them had a different idea than the other two.
So I was a little nervous about this.
It all came back to what had happened somehow.
Somehow it all seemed to stem in some way from what had happened in August of 1956.

My aunt Wendy thought this two-ceremony thing was completely superfluous and that the one at the retirement home was the real one and the main one, and why does Brian need this damn thing in his house?
Uncle Brian thought the retirement home one is the one for the public and it shouldn't be too intense, and the one in his house is the one where we're really going to talk.
But somehow they went off fine.
At the retirement home, I kept it very simple.
I was just the emcee for a gathering and a remembrance and a celebration of life.
I did wear a robe, which I borrowed from Chris because mine's so ratty, so thanks.
I wanted to look my best.
So I just wore a robe and a rakusu, simple priest clothes.
One of my nephews was like, "You look like a monk."
I said, oh, how about that?
There are seven cousins, my son's generation.
People spoke.
It was beautiful.
It was beautiful, at a certain level, like what people were ready for.
My dad talked about how Fran had always made such a big wonderful event of Christmases and birthdays, and she was very DIY.
They had less and less money, especially after he died, and she was very artistic as well.
She would create these fabulous [unclear: "pate-per-mache crushes"], Christmas scenes, scenes of the baby Jesus, really elaborate and detailed.
She was a painter and a sculptor.
That's what he talked about.
He teared up a little bit, but that's what he chose to talk about.
I think my uncle didn't say much at that point.
My aunt said a few things about missing her.
That felt about right.
Then at my uncle's, we went a little further into ritual.
Of course, none of these people had any context of Zen ritual.
They all agreed that I was the one that should do it, because of my connection to Fran and my religious background.
It's weird to me to this day that I could say that.
But they didn't have any context for Zen ritual.
I thought it would be good, it would be helpful, to do some ritual here.
So I made an incense offering and did prostrations.
I hadn't done any of this at the retirement home one.
We set up a little altar with their pictures and the ashes and flowers, and we chanted the [unclear: "Daishin Durrani"].
I brought a little mokugyo, and I was just trying to hold it for everybody.
I gave them copies, and I heard chanting.
I looked down.
I heard people chanting.
There was a melody.
During the chanting, people came up and lit a little tea candle and made this light offering to them and said words if they wanted to.
My sister said some words that were very critical about my father that seemed really inappropriate to me.
So people were working their stuff.
Yeah.
Like forgiving her grandfather for not being the father she needed.
And so the echoes of this.
I mean, she wasn't wrong.
She didn't need to say it quite so loud.
I hope you didn't hear it.
I was right up in front, so maybe I'm the only one who heard all this.
It's like trying to keep chanting.
I should have paused the recorder there.
And then my uncle and my cousin, his daughter, were really ready to speak.
That's where we heard this whole story I'd never heard before about that morning, August 13th, 1956, and how deeply important it was to him.
By then I could see his sister and brother nodding and agreeing and being on the same wavelength as him.
They wouldn't have said all that stuff, but I think they were glad that he did.
This is the day when Fran and Frank are reconnected, when this poem does become true: "You will always be with me.
This grief will always be with me until we meet again."

That really became true the next morning when we went out on this boat, a big wide stable catamaran, out by Point Loma, which was a place they had gone apparently as a family, so it was important to all of them.
It's a lighthouse, a little park.
We're out at sea.
With the help of the people there, I don't know how to do this, but they helped me, we created ten little wicker baskets.
In each basket were their ashes together, and on the top a whole bunch of rose petals.
We gathered in the front of the boat, and I felt like enough words had probably been said already.
It was very quiet going out there, people just quietly talking to each other, resting.
We had a little snack, eating the snack.
So I thought, well, maybe I should just read a poem.
I read this poem by Mary Oliver called "When Death Comes."
I read it twice on the bow of the boat.
Hopefully they could hear it.

*When death comes, like the hungry bear in autumn, when death comes and takes all the bright coins from his purse to buy me and snaps the purse shut, when death comes like the measle pox, when death comes like an iceberg between the shoulder blades, I want to step through the door full of curiosity, wondering, what is it going to be like, that cottage of darkness?
What is it going to be like?*
*And therefore I look upon everything as a brotherhood and a sisterhood, and I look upon time as no more than an idea, and consider eternity as another possibility.
And I think of each life as a flower, as common as a field daisy and a singular, and each name as comfortable music in the mouth, tending, as all music does, towards silence.
And I think of each body as a lion of courage and something precious to the earth.*
*When it's over, I want to say all my life I was a bride married to amazement.
I was the bridegroom taking the world into my arms.
When it's over, I don't want to wonder if I have made something of life...
When it's over, I don't want to wonder if I have made of my life something particular and real.
I don't want to find myself sighing and frightened or full of arguments.
I don't want to end up simply having visited this world.*
I read this poem a couple times, asked if anyone else had any words, and nobody did.

I went to the stern of the boat and sat down there, and the boat person sat down there, and one by one, each of her children and her grandchildren, one of her great-grandchildren actually too, came down and tipped these baskets into the sea.
The ashes just disappear down, like you can see them disappearing down into the water, this white color disappearing into the dark blue-green of the sea.
But then the flower petals float.
Somehow the currents and the wind were such that the flower petals completely surrounded the boat, like a big circle.
Exactly the kind of miracle that I grew up hearing Fran talking about, actually.
Exactly that.
Then no words were needed.
We were just quietly watching the flower petals, all 25 relatives in the boat.
And then, I didn't know who was going to do this, the ship's captain comes out of the control place and rings the ship's bell several times.
I don't know how many times.
Was there a certain number of times?
I didn't count.
Ding, ding.
Exactly what we would have done in here.
I thought, well, maybe that's actually a naval tradition, to ring the ship's bell for a burial at sea.
So I got to do a lot of things in the last month or so.
That was one of the important ones.
I just want to share that.
And just for us to remember, of course, we get by fine.
We're all high-functioning people, more or less.
Not a good day.
But we're all marked by this.
No family is not marked by suffering.
No family can give Kisugatami a mustard seed.
No family hasn't had tragedy.
So therefore, we look upon everyone as a brother and a sister.
Everyone is from that same family, that same family that has known grief and will know grief and sorrow.
Then there are these moments when there's healing.
Might be 60 years later.
You don't know.
The last thing I want to mention is germane to this, but also a ritual and a logistic thing that you should know about.
These little side altars behind me, we put names.
On this altar, we can put names of people who are ill.
Hopefully they'll be okay, but maybe approaching death.
Maybe just temporary illness, but people who are ill.
On this altar, we put people who have passed away.
So a friend's name was there for a while.
Usually you leave the name on the altar for 49 days, and there's a whole story behind why 49 days.

Somebody already mentioned to me tonight that they know or are close to somebody who just died, so I was going to pause a little bit after we bow out in the lobby and come back in here and make a few name cards.
If there's somebody in your life who's ill or has died recently, if you want to come back out, we can make name cards and put them on the altar and do a little ceremony.
But there's something too in doing something together, isn't there?

Whether we employ the ritual language of Zen or some other spiritual discipline, or whether we just make it up or just whatever comes to us, a few words, a breath, a little silence, a little moment of squeeze.
There's something to doing that together with people, the other people from your family that's known grief, or from other families that have known grief.
So may we all heal and may we all be okay in our grief, because that's what we get.
This is our life.
Thank you very much for listening to all that.
It's so nice to be back.

verbatim.text: Good evening everybody. Good to see you. So yeah, usually every year in July I'm supposed to like stop, you know, hovering around here, which is hard for me to do, but I do it and then I appreciate it once I get out the door. So this year during July I did several things. I went on a solo backpack just a couple days with myself and it was really wonderful. I kind of rediscovered something. Some stress fell off, you know. It's amazing how we can carry stress. We don't really notice it, you know, until it releases. And then I went to our Zen monastery in this lineage, Tosahara Monastery in California, and I gave a workshop there on compassion for yourself. That was nice. And then I went to San Diego to see my family, which I'm going to speak about a little bit tonight as a memorial weekend for my grandmother. And then I came back for a second and turned around again and went to Portland, because I thought it would be a good place to experience the heat wave. It was good. It worked out good. Although John did better, I guess, by going to Utah. Hotter there. And there I was at a meeting of the American Zen Teachers Association.

Are you going to let me be okay with the fan on or should we turn it off? It's nice to have the air, huh? Okay. Who cares? You can hear me. And that was really, I didn't really want to go because I've been away so much, but I was really glad I went to that meeting, four day meeting. People from all over the country and different Zen lineages, not just our Soto Zen school, but different stripes and varieties of Zen. And it was hosted at a Zen temple in a different lineage, a place called Dharma Reign Zen Community, which is an amazing place. I'll say more about that another time, but really good. I really recommend. It's really great to be a Zen tourist and go to different centers and give you a little more perspective on what we're doing here. And Colette and Jonathan were saying they were just Zen tourists too. They went to the Greenville Farms Zen Center in California. And it's really fun. On the one hand, you appreciate the different ways that they do things in these different Zen places.

Like kind of familiar, but kind of different, you know. And then your mind often usually goes off on the stupid way that they do things because it's not what you're used to, right? So if it's not what you're used to, it must not be right. And then your mind spins around from there and you say, what a dummy I am for thinking that. It's perfectly legitimate. I should respect diversity. So it's one of my favorite things about this whole enterprise that we take so seriously the particulars and details of the way we do things, because it matters and there's a feeling to it.
